A Weighting Argument for Pointwise Convergence to Convergence in Measure

Henry Shin · May 7, 2026 · revised September 22, 2026

Measure theory and convergence of measurable functions.

  • Short route: dominated convergence Section 4 proves L¹ convergence and hence convergence in measure.
  • Stronger route: conull uniformity Sections 2–3 construct a different weight giving uniform convergence outside a null set.

The mechanism

Change the scale at each point

Pointwise information need not give uniform control. This argument introduces a positive measurable weight that adjusts the scale from point to point. The weighted sequence can then be controlled using a decomposition argument or dominated convergence.

What becomes elementary: Choosing the weight turns local convergence information into a statement about the measure of exceptional sets.

For the shortest proof of the title’s conclusion, use the dominated-convergence argument in §4: it gives convergence in L¹ and hence in measure. The construction in §§2–3 does more work to obtain uniform convergence on a conull set. In each route, track positivity and measurability of the weight.

Explore further constructions. Edition dates, sources and reference chapters identify the scope of each study.

Overview

Let be a sequence of real-valued Lebesgue measurable functions on such that for every . We give a detailed proof that there exists a strictly positive measurable function such that in measure. The main proof is an expanded version of a Math StackExchange answer of the author: it uses a finite-measure exhaustion, Egorov’s theorem on each finite-measure piece, and a pointwise-boundedness stratification. The construction actually proves the stronger conclusion that uniformly on a conull measurable subset of . We also include a shorter dominated-convergence proof of the original statement and record the corresponding sigma-finite version.

1 · Introduction

On a finite measure space, almost everywhere convergence implies convergence in measure. On an infinite measure space, such as with Lebesgue measure, this implication is false in general. The problem considered here asks whether one can multiply by a positive measurable weight in order to force convergence in measure.

The answer is yes. More precisely, if are measurable and pointwise, then there is a strictly positive measurable function such that

in measure. The construction below proves something stronger: can be chosen so that uniformly on a measurable set whose complement has Lebesgue measure zero.

The key idea is to combine two elementary consequences of pointwise convergence. First, after decomposing into countably many finite-measure sets, Egorov’s theorem gives countably many large pieces on which the convergence is uniform. Second, at each fixed point , the scalar sequence is bounded, so is the union of the level sets on which the pointwise envelope is bounded. The weight is then made small on the intersections of these two decompositions.

6 · Concluding remarks

The Egorov construction combines two countable stratifications:

  1. pieces on which convergence is uniform, supplied here by Egorov’s theorem on finite-measure pieces;

  2. pieces on which the whole sequence is uniformly bounded, supplied here by the pointwise envelope .

The weight is then chosen small enough on the intersections of the two stratifications. The role of sigma-finiteness is precisely to make the first stratification countable through finite-measure exhaustion. The role of pointwise convergence is not only to give the limiting value , but also to guarantee pointwise boundedness of the sequence, which is what makes the second stratification possible.
